Our Father
OWR FAH-ther
n. phrase (the opening address of the Lord's Prayer, Matthew 6:9; the Trinitarian name of God as Father revealed by Christ)
Father from Old English fæder, from Proto-Germanic *fader, cognate with Latin pater, Greek patēr, Sanskrit pitā. The pronoun “our” from Old English āre. The address “Our Father” (Greek Pater hēmōn) in Matthew 6:9 is the specific covenant address Jesus teaches His disciples to use in prayer. It is distinguished from the general theological concept of divine fatherhood by its prayer-address character: it is the name by which the elect approach the First Person of the Trinity through the mediation of the Son.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

When Jesus teaches His disciples to address God as “Our Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 6:9), He does something unprecedented in Old Testament piety. While Israel knew God as Father in a covenantal-national sense (Isaiah 63:16; 64:8; Deuteronomy 32:6) and individual psalms use filial language, the address “Father” was not the characteristic prayer-address of Old Testament prayer. Jesus' own distinctive practice — addressing God as Abba, the Aramaic familial term for father (Mark 14:36) — is the ground for the disciples' address. The Son's unique Sonship (Matthew 11:27: “no one knows the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son wills to reveal Him”) is the basis on which believers may approach God as Father: they pray to “our Father” because they are adopted into the Son's relation with the Father through regeneration and faith. Galatians 4:6 confirms: “Because you are sons, God has sent forth the Spirit of His Son into our hearts — crying out, 'Abba! Father!'” The Spirit of adoption enables the believer's cry to the Father. The address “Our Father” is therefore not merely polite address or general theism; it is the adoptive privilege of those who have been brought into the family of God through union with the eternal Son. The word “our” also establishes the communal character of Christian prayer: we pray not as isolated individuals but as members of the one covenant family of God, sharing one Father, one inheritance, and one hope.

Webster 1828 Definition

The address “Our Father” (Matthew 6:9) is not merely polite theistic address but the adoptive privilege of those united to the Son — the Spirit of adoption enabling the believer's cry to the First Person of the Trinity through the Son's own mediation.

OUR FATHER, n. [Old English fæder; Greek Pater hēmōn.] The opening address of the Lord's Prayer (Matthew 6:9), prescribed by Christ as the pattern of covenant approach to God the Father. It is not a general divine title but the specific adoptive address enabled by the Son's mediation and the Spirit's work of adoption.

The Old Testament prepared for but did not fully establish the “Father” address in prayer. Israel called God Father in a covenantal-national sense (Deut. 32:6; Isa. 63:16) but the characteristic Old Testament prayer address is “LORD” (YHWH) or “God” (El/Elohim). Jesus' own practice of addressing God as Abba (Mark 14:36) was a distinctive intensification that shocked His contemporaries.

Matthew 11:27 is the theological key: “No one knows the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son wills to reveal Him.” Access to the Father-address requires Sonship revealed through Christ. The disciples' “Our Father” is not self-acquired; it is adopted privilege, received through union with the eternal Son who alone knows the Father by nature.

Galatians 4:6 and Romans 8:15 describe the Spirit's role in enabling the Father-address: the Spirit of adoption makes the believer cry “Abba, Father” — a participation in the Son's own communion with the Father. The “Our Father” of the Lord's Prayer is not rote repetition; it is the Spirit-prompted cry of the adopted child entering the presence of the adopting God.

The communal pronoun “our” guards against individualism in prayer: Christians do not approach God as solitary petitioners with private rights but as members of the one household of God. To say “Our Father” is to acknowledge the whole covenant family, to pray in solidarity with every other adopted child, and to approach the One who is equally the Father of all who belong to Christ.

Key Scripture

Matthew 6:9 — "Pray, then, in this way: 'Our Father who is in heaven, hallowed be Your name."

Matthew 11:27 — "All things have been handed over to Me by My Father — and no one knows the Son, except the Father. Nor does anyone know the Father, except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son wills to reveal Him."

Galatians 4:6 — "And because you are sons, God has sent forth the Spirit of His Son into our hearts — crying out, “Abba! Father!”"

John 17:1 — "When Jesus had said these things, He lifted up His eyes to heaven and said: “Father, the hour has come. Glorify Your Son, so that the Son may glorify You —"

Modern Corruption

Feminist liturgy corrupts the “Our Father” address by substituting gender-neutral or maternal language — denying that “Father” is the name revealed by Christ and not merely a cultural metaphor; Open Theism strips the Father-address of its covenantal security by denying the Father's exhaustive foreknowledge.

expand to see more

The feminist liturgical project — represented by Elisabeth Schüssler Fiorenza, Sallie McFague (Models of God, 1987), and the Inclusive Language Lectionary tradition — treats “Our Father” as a patriarchal cultural projection onto deity rather than the name revealed by the Son. McFague proposed “Mother,” “Lover,” and “Friend” as equally valid models for God, dissolving the revealed name into a preference menu. This fails on the most basic point: Jesus did not teach His disciples to address God by a culturally appropriate metaphor of their choosing; He taught them to address God by the name the Son revealed. The Father-Son relation is not a figure of speech; it is the inner-Trinitarian ground of all prayer.

Open Theism (Clark Pinnock, Greg Boyd, John Sanders) undermines the “Our Father” address from the other direction: if the Father does not possess exhaustive foreknowledge of the future, the creature's prayer becomes a collaboration of equals attempting to navigate an open future rather than a child approaching an omniscient, all-wise, sovereign Father who “knows what you need before you ask Him” (Matthew 6:8). The Lord's Prayer presupposes a Father who knows, governs, and can grant; Open Theism gives the child an uncertain colleague rather than an omnipotent Father.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The “Our Father” address flows from the Son's unique knowledge of the Father (Matthew 11:27), through the Spirit of adoption (Galatians 4:6; Romans 8:15), and is grounded in the eternal Trinitarian relation that the Son's incarnation reveals to and applies for the elect.

expand to see more

Old Testament preparations (Deuteronomy 32:6; Isaiah 63:16; 64:8) — Israel's covenantal-national fatherhood language prepares the category without establishing the adoptive intimacy; these texts call God Father in the sense of Creator and covenant head, not the intimate access Christ opens.

Matthew 11:27 (exclusive knowledge) — the Son's unique and mutual knowledge of the Father is the theological ground for the disciples' address; only those to whom the Son reveals the Father can pray “Our Father.”

Romans 8:15 and Galatians 4:6 (Spirit of adoption) — the Spirit who cries “Abba, Father” in the believer's heart is the same Spirit of the Son; the adopted children share the Son's prayer vocabulary because they share the Son's Spirit.

High-priestly prayer (John 17) — Jesus' own address to the Father in John 17 models the intimate, confident, covenant-grounded approach He teaches the disciples; “Holy Father” and “righteous Father” nuance the address with holiness and justice.

Westminster Shorter Catechism Q. 100 — “The preface of the Lord's Prayer teacheth us to draw near to God with all holy reverence and confidence, as children to a father, able and ready to help us”; the catechism distills the adoptive confidence the address is designed to instill.

Usage

"To say “Our Father” with understanding is to make a Trinitarian claim: the Father addressed is the First Person of the Trinity, known only through the Son, approached only by the Spirit of adoption; every genuine prayer to the Father is therefore Trinitarian prayer, whether or not the structure is explicit."

"The communal “our” rebukes private-religion Christianity: Christians do not have a personal Father distinct from the church's Father; to pray “Our Father” is to include the whole covenant family in the approach and to refuse the individualism that treats prayer as a private transaction."

"The progressive feminist project to replace “Father” in the Lord's Prayer reveals its deepest assumption: that the Creator's revealed name is negotiable. Jesus taught one specific address — the name the Son gives to the one He knows by nature; to change it is to claim the authority to rename the God who has already named Himself."
